content: Separation anxiety disorder is a psychological condition characterized by excessive anxiety regarding separation from home or from individuals to whom the person has a strong emotional attachment, such as a parent or caregiver. This condition often coexists with other mental health disorders. Research indicates that children diagnosed with separation anxiety disorder are at a significantly higher risk of developing conditions such as ADHD, bipolar disorder, panic disorder, and others later in life. It is important to distinguish separation anxiety disorder from separation anxiety, the latter being a normal developmental stage observed in healthy, securely attached infants. Separation anxiety typically arises as infants begin to understand their individuality—that they are separate entities from their primary caregivers. Concurrently, they start to develop the concept of object permanence, which is the understanding that objects or people continue to exist even when they are not visible or audible. However, during this developmental stage, infants do not yet comprehend that their caregiver will return after a separation, nor do they have a clear understanding of time. This lack of understanding can lead to a normal and healthy anxious reaction. Separation anxiety disorder can occur across all age groups. In adults, it is more prevalent, affecting approximately 7% of the population, compared to childhood separation anxiety disorder, which affects about 4% of children.
